Raku firing is loud and messy, and the smoke always sends him inside coughing for an hour. He is preparing for a fundraiser at the community center where local politicians will bid on his work. The mayor has already asked whether he can make a pitcher with a crooked spout.

The clay in the bucket has gone stiff from sitting over the long weekend away. He has been reading about old Korean ash glazes and experimenting with rice husks in a batch of test tiles. Moving to a smaller house took most of his evenings, yet the workbench came along intact.

He presses his thumb into the wet rim of a jar and feels for the exact thickness he wants. A friend from work recently asked him for a planter and he is still deciding on the shape. His old school friend wrote him a letter asking about his kiln, which he answered at the kitchen table.

Wheel throwing takes years to feel natural, and he still fumbles when the clay slips off center. The new commuter rail stop near his apartment has brought more walkers past the studio window. He waves at passersby, sometimes holding up a glazed cup for them to see.

Between firings he sands the foot rings of his bowls until they sit flat on any table. At the library last week he gave a talk about the history of local brickworks, mostly to a small crowd of retirees. His cough returned halfway through, which made the audience laugh with him.

The kiln groans as it heats past a thousand degrees and he keeps one eye on the pyrometer. His son asked him to help paint a mural for the new school gymnasium. The paint smell gave him a headache that lasted until the next morning.

Local elections always drag him into arguments at the hardware store about funding for the arts. He would rather be trimming pots, but the council decided to cut the pottery program at the high school. He wrote three letters and then went back to the wheel to calm down.

In summer the studio door stays open and moths drift in around the lamp while he glazes. He is teaching a weekend class for beginners who arrive with coffee and no idea how to center clay. Their first bowls wobble badly, and he tells them that is perfectly normal.

A dry sense of humor runs through everything he makes, from lopsided mugs to deliberately odd teapots. He lost a bet with his brother over a college football game and had to deliver a set of soup bowls as payment. The bowls arrived with a note saying they were all his fault.

Between spells of illness he returns to the studio and throws until the light fades from the window. The move to the new flat left him with an unfamiliar kitchen, so he cooks eggs on a hot plate beside the kiln. Friends bring him soup while he tries to finish a set of teacups.

He keeps his wheel in the back room of the flat, and the clay he buys comes in twenty-five kilo sacks that he drags up the stairs himself. Last winter the radiator died and he threw bowls with gloves on. His landlord still hasn't fixed it.

Most evenings after the warehouse shift he sits at the wheel with wet hands and a stubborn mug that keeps collapsing. Glaze runs down the sides of his sink in purple streaks. He says the night shifts have made him slower but more patient with the clay.

The kiln sits in the garage like a metal wardrobe, humming on its timer. He fires it once a fortnight and waits for the cones to slump before he opens the lid. Since the move he has not found a place nearly as good for it.

Mostly he makes plates now, because they dry flat and forgive mistakes. His sister bought one at the church fair and he was quietly pleased. The new phone takes photos of the glaze better than the old one did, which he mentions more than once.

There is a shelf of his pots at the community centre where the councillors hold their meetings. Nobody has bought anything yet, though a woman from the planning committee once turned a mug over and checked the base. He thinks that counts as interest.

His doctor told him to ease off the heavy lifting, so he now buys smaller bags of clay and does his wedging on a board. The wrist still aches after a long session at the wheel. He keeps a hot water bottle on the stool beside him anyway.

A chipped rim on his favourite jug got him thinking about repair. He mended it with a thin gold line and felt faintly foolish, then rather proud. The flat has a damp patch above the cooker that the landlord keeps promising to look at.

Clay dust settles on everything in the flat, including the bread he leaves out on the counter. He wipes down the kitchen twice a week and still finds grit in the tea. Since the move he has accepted that living with clay means living with clay.

Some weeks the kiln fails and everything comes out grey and sad, and he sits on the back step smoking nothing. The council cut the funding for the studio that used to share the firing costs. He says he will manage, which is what people say when they are not sure.

The newest bowls have a celadon glaze that took him four attempts to get right. Each failed test went into a bucket by the bins, a small heap of mistakes. The landlord once asked what the buckets were for and he did not really have an answer.

He sells a few pieces through a shop near the old station, taking a cut that he resents but accepts. The shopkeeper complains about the heavy stoneware but orders more every spring. In quiet moments he thinks about the first pot he ever made, lopsided and proud.

At the wheel he forgets the rent, the cough, the new phone's constant notifications. The clay asks for steady hands and a clear head, so for an hour the rest of his life waits outside the door. When he finishes he always looks around the room as though someone else has come in.

A neighbour's child wandered in last month and asked why the bowls had fingerprints in them. He explained centring and pressure in plain words, and the child nodded as if it all made perfect sense. He has been thinking about that conversation ever since.

Local politics has him grumbling more than usual, mostly about the parking charges outside the studio. He wrote a letter to the paper and nobody replied, which he took with weary good humour. Then he went back to the wheel and centred a fresh lump of clay.

Winter brings condensation on the window and cracks in the cheaper glazes that he refuses to sell. He wraps the drying pieces in plastic like sleeping animals and checks them each morning. The flat is cold enough that his breath shows near the sink.

He made a set of pots for his father before the funeral, and he kept one for himself. The glaze on it has crazed slightly over the years, a web of fine lines he decided not to fix. It sits on the windowsill where the afternoon sun catches it.

A man from the tenants association came round asking about the damp, and he showed him the photographs on the new phone. The man nodded slowly and wrote things in a notebook. Afterwards he returned to his stool and threw a tall vase that wobbled but stood.

Tomorrow he will unload the kiln and see what survived, the way he does every fortnight. Some pieces will be perfect, some will be ruined, and most will be somewhere in between. He puts the kettle on and waits for the sound of the kiln cooling.

Pottery is the only thing he does that makes his hands look like they belong to someone useful. His glaze buckets sit beside the kettle, and his savings jar for a deposit on a house has gotten a little heavier each month. Friends have stopped asking whether he is still doing the mugs.

The kiln is his real pride, a dented old electric thing he rewired himself after the last landlord refused. He trims leather hard bowls with a wire tool and talks to the glaze as if it might listen. At work his colleague keeps asking when the next firing is.

Every spring he hauls a box of stoneware to the community craft market and sells maybe half of it. The council has been arguing about the rent on the unit, and he has written two letters that nobody answered. His old school friend bought a chipped teapot and promised to bring his own clay next time.

Throwing on the wheel is where he goes to forget the phone buzzing in his pocket. He does his best work with the radio off, listening to the wheel hum and the water drip into the slop bucket. The new phone has a camera he uses only to photograph finished glazes for his notebook.

The studio smells of wet grog and cold tea, and nobody minds much. He glazes slowly, dipping each piece twice, then wiping the foot ring clean with a damp sponge. He is saving for a proper extruder, though the upstairs flat has been loud enough lately to make him doubt the sums.

The wheel sits by the window, so he sees the neighbourhood petition come and go. He signed it, mostly because the bus stop near his studio keeps getting worse. Pottery gives him something that stays put when everything else is in flux.

Clay dust settles on every surface of the spare room, and the new mortgage calculator sits open on his laptop beside the kiln log. He throws in short bursts, then stops to check the figures. A friend from his old band asked if he wanted to sell a set of bowls to a restaurant.

He keeps the wheel head perfectly level and checks it with a spirit level each time he sets up. A coworker jokes that he should be building a house instead of cups. He takes the joke well, having already sketched a kitchen on the back of a glaze chart.

Most of his evenings disappear into trimming, drying and waiting for the kiln to cool. The flat above him has a dog that runs laps at midnight, which has taught him to keep his hands steady. His mother still has the first bowl he ever made, lopsided and proud.

Pottery became his way of sitting still, which he had not expected from a man who used to fix engines for a living. He makes thick pinch pots for the kids on the estate and lets them paint the glaze. Somewhere in the back of his mind is the house deposit, growing slow and steady.

The kiln fires overnight, so he sleeps badly on firing nights and wakes up checking the gauge on his new phone. He trims a row of small vases with a loop tool. A local politician once visited the studio and asked him to explain clay to the planning committee.

He weighs every lump of clay on a cheap kitchen scale before he throws, aiming for the same size each time. A neighbour from the flat downstairs bought a bowl and complained about the noise, then came back for two more. The savings account grows a little each time a piece sells.

Throwing a tall jar is the hardest thing he does, and he still gets it wrong about half the time. He keeps a sponge, a rib and a bucket of slip within reach. His old friend from school texts him photos of their children and asks what he is firing this week.

His favourite pieces are the ones that crack in the kiln and teach him something new about shrinkage. He keeps the failures on a shelf, labelled in pencil. Lately his brother has been asking him to make a set of mugs for the new flat they are buying together.

Most afternoons find him kneading a block of porcelain on the old wooden table by the window. The porcelain is stubborn, and it cracks at the rim if the pressure is uneven. A new phone sits face down beside his stool, forgotten while he trims a bowl to a whisper of thickness.

Slip trailed down the side of a wide serving platter is his current obsession. He lets it dry to the color of weak tea before firing it in the electric kiln downstairs. The landlord complained about the fumes last month, so he now opens every window before lighting the kiln.

The studio in his new apartment has a north facing window that makes the glazes look different every hour. He stacks finished pieces on plank shelves, each one wrapped in newspaper from the old house. His sister visited last weekend and bought a small dish with a crackled blue finish.

He tends to work late into the evening when the streets outside go quiet and the cafe across the road closes its shutters. A row of drying bisque ware waits on the windowsill, pale and fragile. He hums while he trims, and the sound fills the small room comfortably.

Visitors often find him dusting a glaze test tile with a soft brush while the kettle boils. He keeps a jar of ash from a friend's fireplace for a special celluloid like finish. The town council recently debated a new kiln ordinance, and he sent a long letter that made the local paper.

His latest project is a set of tea bowls with uneven rims and a rough sandy texture. He worries the glaze might pool in the base, so he checks each one twice before loading the kiln. Regular walks to the cafe help him clear his head between firings.

A stack of cracked pieces sits in a bucket beside the wheel, a reminder of the batches that went wrong. He does not throw them away, since he grinds them into grog for the next mix. The new phone he bought sits charging in the kitchen, rarely checked during working hours.

Summer means long afternoons in the open shed behind the house, where the air smells of warm earth. He throws vases with thin walls and watches them stiffen under a sheet of plastic. Recently he has been cutting back on coffee, so the cafe visits have become a treat rather than a habit.

His grandfather taught him to center clay on a kick wheel in a cold shed years ago. Those early bowls were lopsided and heavy, and he still keeps one on a shelf near the door. Local elections have made the whole town tense, but he mostly talks about glaze chemistry.

Pottery takes up most of his weekends now, and his partner has stopped asking where all the sawdust comes from. He recently glazed a set of tea bowls in a deep blue that he has been chasing for years. The old family dog snores under the table while he works on yet another test tile.

The kiln hums through the night, and he checks the temperature gauge every few hours to be safe. He recently sold a small batch of mugs at a local market, and the money went straight into the house fund. The noisy flat above sometimes goes quiet, and he appreciates the peace when it does.

He spends his afternoons carving decorative patterns into leather hard vases with a sharpened loop tool. The kids find the curls of clay he leaves on the floor endlessly fascinating and sweep them up into jars. His dog naps on the old rug nearby, sometimes stealing a stray bit of slip.

Each firing brings a new surprise, and he has learned to accept the cracked pieces as part of the process. The upstairs neighbours recently replaced their floorboards, which made the whole flat shake for a week. He keeps a small jar of saved coins labelled house deposit next to his glaze buckets.

The weather in March is still cold enough that his glazes take forever to dry on the rack by the window. He has started trimming his bowls with a steel loop tool that his grandfather once owned. On the long drive in from the suburbs, he rehearses which glaze he wants to try next.

Pottery has taught him patience in a way his job never did. He throws cylinders in the mornings before his sister calls about dinner plans. Each mug he makes has a slightly different foot ring, and he says that is the whole point.

He bought a secondhand electric wheel from a retiring art teacher across the river. The motor still whines when he pushes the pedal too hard. His neighbors have started leaving empty cardboard boxes by the curb, which he uses to protect finished pieces on the drive home.

Most evenings he wedges a fresh batch of stoneware on a canvas board in the garage. The smell of wet clay drifts into the kitchen where his father is reading the paper. After glazing, he waits anxiously for the kiln to cool before opening the lid.

On rainy afternoons he sits under the carport and trims leather hard bowls while the gutters overflow. His landlord once asked whether the dust would damage the paint, and he promised to sweep twice a week. The commute to the studio takes forty minutes, but the drive is worth it for the quiet.

The studio on Maple Street has a cracked skylight that lets in thin streaks of sun. He spends hours there pulling handles onto teapot lids and adjusting spouts until they pour cleanly. Afterward he cleans the splash pan and feels oddly content.

Clay dust settles on the windowsill of his tiny apartment no matter how often he sweeps. He does not mind, since the mess is part of the process. His upstairs neighbor complained once about the banging, so he now throws mostly in the early morning.

In the summer heat he works barefoot on a cool tile floor and listens to a ballgame on an old radio. A slab of porcelain sits drying on the table, warping slightly as the afternoon warms. He is hoping it will hold together in the kiln.

He joined a small pottery guild that meets above the hardware store on the corner of Fifth. The members trade glaze tips over burnt coffee and argue about which clay bodies shrink least. He always leaves with a bag of fresh slip.

Each spring the pottery sale at the park brings out a crowd of families, and he sets up a folding table with his crooked vases. The weather turned windy last year and nearly toppled everything. His parents came to help him count the cash at the end of the day.

When he moved into the old farmhouse, the landlord agreed to add a ventilation fan above the kiln shed. Now the fumes do not seep into the living room. He glazes on the porch in the late afternoon while crickets start to sing.

He throws bowls that look a little lopsided and sometimes he likes them that way. A friend from work once asked why he doesn't make perfect symmetrical plates, and he just shrugged. The wheel does what it wants and he follows.

Every December he stacks the kiln with mugs for the family holiday exchange, a tradition his sister insists on. The glaze turns a deep green when fired properly. He wraps each mug in newspaper and writes names on the bottoms with a pencil.

A small cracked bowl sits on his nightstand, a reminder that the kiln can be unforgiving. He still uses it for keys and loose change. The landlord who rents him the studio space asked him to share a few tips for beginners.

Winter nights in the apartment are cold, so he sets his kiln to fire while he reads by the window. The radiator clanks as the heat rises. In the morning he unpacks glazed tumblers that gleam like polished stones.

He spends most of his evenings at the wheel in the back room, where the kiln hums like a fridge that never switches off. His landlord has stopped asking what the smell is. The clay he buys is the cheap stoneware, and he says the good stuff just makes him nervous.

The glaze on his mugs is a dull green that he calls celadon, though his coworker insists it looks like pond water. He sands the feet of every piece by hand. Night shifts at the warehouse leave him with nothing to do but wait for the kiln to cool.

Kiln firing takes him the better part of a day, and he checks the cones through a small peephole with the seriousness of a surgeon. A friend from work offered to help load it and got stuck with the heavy shelves. He never forgets to wipe down the wheel head afterwards.

There is a stubborn streak in him that shows most when a pot slumps in the bisque firing. He puts it back on the shelf and tries again the next week. His landlord once asked whether he sold anything, and he said only to people who ask nicely.

The thumb-pressed bowls he makes have a lopsided charm that sells better than the tidy ones. He does not really believe that, but he does not argue with the buyers at the craft fair. His coworker bought two and now uses them for pens.

Upstairs a family plays loud music late into the night, so he works in the mornings instead. The clay is softer then and easier to coax. He finds that the bowls turn out better when he is not tired, which is obvious but still surprises him.
He throws pots in the same grey smock every time, now stiff with dried slip. His sister says it looks like he has been dipped in porridge. The smock stays because it knows where all the pockets are.

A cracked rim does not end a piece for him, he simply learns to live with the line. He mends them with gold lustre and considers them finished. His landlord, who has no interest in pottery, once said it looked like a repair kit.

His studio is a converted garage with a drain in the floor and a radio on the windowsill. He keeps it tuned to a station that plays old folk songs. Between shifts at the depot he spends hours wedging clay on a plaster slab.

Glazing is the part he dislikes most, because the buckets stain his hands for days. Once a fortnight he stands over a dipping bucket and counts under his breath. His coworker calls it his monthly baptism.

Visitors usually ask about the kiln first, the big steel box that dominates the back room and roars like a boiler. He lets them open the lid when it has cooled. His sister has never asked what it costs to run, which he appreciates.

He sells the odd bowl through a small online shop he set up after a long night shift. Packing them in newspaper takes longer than making them. The news about the rising price of electricity has made him think twice about firing more often.

The pottery class he still attends meets in a church hall with mismatched chairs and a stained carpet. He is the oldest student there and the one who asks the most questions. The teacher once told him his pots had the honesty of a farmhouse table.

He labels every piece with a small stamp on the base, a crude spiral he cut from a biscuit tin lid. The stamp has worn thin over the years but he refuses to replace it. His sister says it looks like something a child would make, which is exactly why he likes it.

Nobody expected the bowl to survive the kiln, least of all him. The crackle glaze came out gray instead of blue, and he is still sulking about it. He has a cold this week, so the studio stays quiet and the wheel sits unused.

The studio smells of wet stoneware and burnt wax when he opens the door. He trims leather hard pots with a metal loop tool and keeps a bucket of slip beside the table. Because he works night shifts at the hospital, he throws his pots at seven in the morning, when the building is still calm.

On rainy afternoons he sits near the window of his favorite cafe with a sketchbook full of rim profiles and foot ring ideas. The waiter knows him well enough to bring the good tea without asking. He draws quickly, then goes home to test the shapes on the wheel.

The kiln runs overnight, and he checks the cones through a peephole before bed. Last winter a power cut ruined an entire firing, so he now keeps a flashlight and a spare plug by the door. He is careful about these things in a way his friends find amusing.

Stoneware clay is cheaper if you buy it by the fifty pound bag, he explains while carrying one up the stairs. He wedges it on a canvas board and rolls it into long coils for hand building. His back aches afterward, and he has started taking a heating pad to the studio.

He has been experimenting with wood firing, which means stacking hundreds of pieces in a brick chamber and feeding it logs for days. The ash settles on the surfaces and makes the glaze look like tree bark. He tells everyone it is worth the lost sleep, though his sister disagrees.

A cracked tile from the old studio floor sits on his shelf as a reminder of his first failed experiment. He learned that bisque firing must be slow enough to drive out water. These days he tapes a note to the kiln reminding himself to vent it.

He once tried making teapots and gave up after the lids kept falling off. The spouts clogged, the handles drooped, and he cursed the whole project. Now he sticks to bowls, which forgive more mistakes and let him focus on the glaze.

His new phone has a timer app he uses to remind himself when a piece should leave the wheel. It has also helped him track the drying times for different clays. He jokes that technology has made him a more patient potter.

The studio is a converted garage with a wobbly shelf, a radio that only picks up one station, and a row of bowls drying on newspaper. He likes the clutter, because it proves the place is used. Visitors often assume it is a hobby for retirees, which amuses him.

He throws a few mugs for the cafe down the street every spring, and they keep the order on the counter. The owner asked him to match a particular blue glaze, which took him four tests to get right. Now the cafe staff use his mugs for every latte.

He treasures a secondhand Japanese kick wheel that his grandfather once used for repairing ceramic tiles. The wheel squeaks, and he oils it every month. He says it throws more smoothly than any electric machine he has tried.

The most frustrating part of pottery, he says, is waiting for a bowl to dry evenly before trimming it. He covers pieces with plastic overnight and checks them with the back of his hand. He once lost a whole morning to a pot that warped in the rain.

A pottery class he taught at the community center left him exhausted but grateful. His students kept asking how to center clay, and he kept demonstrating with his sore wrists. Afterward he treated himself to a cold drink and a long nap.

The clay he buys comes in fifty pound sacks that he drags in from the van without complaint. He throws mugs mostly, and the handles never match, which he says is the point. Work at the depot leaves him tired, but the wheel calms him down.

Glaze is his real obsession, the blue that only comes out right in the reduction firing. Lately he has been testing tiles on a board pinned to the garage wall. Nobody asked him to keep records, but he does anyway.

Once a year the local craft fair gives him a folding table and a bad spot near the restrooms. He sells maybe a dozen pieces and gives away the rest to his old friend from school. The friend keeps everything on a shelf above the stove.

Nights on the ambulance crew leave him wide awake at odd hours, so he finds himself centering clay at four in the morning. The studio smells of wet earth and burnt wood from the kiln. Sleep comes later, usually after breakfast.

He donated a stack of serving bowls to the library fundraiser when the council cut the budget again. The town meeting had been loud and nobody agreed on much. Pottery seemed like the one thing he could fix with his hands.

The old kick wheel in his garage belonged to his late father, who taught him to pull walls thin enough to see the light. He still uses the same worn wooden rib, now stained darker than the clay. Some afternoons he just sits and listens to the wheel turn.

He signed up for a weekend workshop in another state and came back with ideas he is still trying out. The instructor kept saying the clay tells you what it wants. He now repeats that line to anyone who asks about his shelves.

Each winter he loses a few pieces to cracks in the kiln, and he treats the ruined ones like a small funeral. He keeps the shards in a cardboard box labeled with the firing date. Nobody else knows why.

He once gave a neighbor a vase after the neighbor's house burned down, and the neighbor kept it on the mantel for years. He never mentioned it again. The vase has a small chip near the base, which he never fixed.

On slow evenings he sketches new shapes on the back of old invoices while his wife reads in the next room. The pencil marks drift from jug to bowl to something he cannot name yet. He tears the pages out and stacks them by the door.

The studio heater broke during the cold snap, so he worked in a parka with fingerless gloves. The clay kept stiffening faster than he could shape it. He finished one bowl anyway and set it on the windowsill to dry.

A younger man from the depot asked him to show how to trim a foot ring, and he spent an afternoon guiding the younger man's hands. The younger man left with a crooked bowl and a grin. He hung the bowl on his own hook above the door.

Stories about his grandfather who made bricks in a yard across the river drift through his thinking when he works the clay. He never knew that man well, but the red dust on his boots feels familiar. He tells his children about it at dinner, rarely in order.

Under the kiln's glow his hands look older than they are. He throws slowly and talks even more slowly about the glaze he never quite perfected. His grandfather once carved wooden spoons in a cramped shed, and sometimes he thinks of that shed while centering a lump of stoneware.

The clay has to be wedged before anything else happens, and he does this with a kind of stubborn patience. Last spring he moved into a rental with a tiny studio out back. His coworker asked why he bothers, and he shrugged and said the work keeps him honest.

He stacks his drying pots on wooden shelves like a careful librarian. The studio smells of damp earth and a little burnt sugar from the firing. Some evenings he scrolls through his new phone, comparing other potters' glazes with his own sad attempts.

Nobody in the family expected him to stick with it. A bowl that cracked in the bisque firing still sits on his windowsill, a reminder of school art classes where he first pressed his thumb into soft clay. He laughs about it now, mostly.

His favorite mug has a lopsided handle and a glaze that pools a little too thick near the foot. He drinks his morning coffee from it while the sun rises over the parking lot. An old friend once called it ugly, and he still considers that a compliment.

There is a particular silence in the studio when the wheel spins fast and true. He dislikes the noise of traffic outside, so he keeps the radio low. A recent move across town means a longer drive to the supply shop, which he grumbles about in every conversation.

The dust from the trimming tools settles on his shoulders by the end of the day. He tells people the work is meditative, which is true, but also mostly just messy. A former colleague who now runs a bakery asked him to make a set of custom dishes.

Each glaze test gets a tiny label in faded marker. He has a drawer full of tiles that never turned out right. His old high school teacher once told him he had a good eye, and he thinks about that when he chooses the color.

On quiet mornings he sits on a stool by the kiln and listens to it hum. He has been thinking about selling his pieces online, though the thought makes him anxious. A cousin recently moved in nearby and drops by to admire the stacked bisque ware.

The studio window fogs up in winter from the warm kiln. He wipes it with a dry rag and looks out at the empty street. A memory of his grandfather's rough hands guiding his own over a spinning block of clay comes back to him.

He weighs each lump of clay on an old kitchen scale before he throws it. The pieces he makes are heavier than they look, which people always notice when they pick one up. His neighbor complained about the noise once, and he apologized, then went right back to the wheel.

Some of his best ideas come while he scrubs the wheel head clean at night. He sings badly under his breath and forgets the words halfway through. A friend from his old job asked him to teach a weekend class, and he is still deciding.

The glaze buckets line the back wall like a row of tiny paint cans. He mixes them by hand with a whisk that has seen better days. He does not own a television, which his brother finds baffling, but he does own a very good kiln.

After the firing he unpacks each piece slowly, almost reverently, checking for cracks and crazing. Nothing about the process is fast. He once broke a whole batch in a fit of frustration, and his old roommate still brings it up at parties.

When the weather turns cold he moves his drying racks closer to the space heater. The clay stays workable longer that way, though he worries about the cost of electricity. He found the studio through a flyer tacked to a bulletin board at work.

A small wooden sign above the sink reads simply clean as you go, a gift from his grandfather. He tries to follow it, though the wet clay has other ideas. Lately he has been thinking about retiring from his day job to throw full time.

His grandfather taught him to throw on a foot-powered wheel in a damp shed. Now he uses an electric one that spins too fast for his liking. He still pushes his thumb into the centre of every pot the way the old man did, slowly and without fuss.

Some evenings after his shift at the warehouse, he slumps at the wheel and just lets the clay turn. Glazing takes patience he doesn't always have, so the mugs pile up half finished on the shelf. Still, the smell of wet earth settles him better than anything else.

He wedged the clay by hand this morning while the radio murmured about traffic. His wrists ache a bit more than they used to, and the doctor has suggested he ease off, though he has not. The vase he made last month is finally drying properly on the windowsill.

At the cafe down the road, he sits near the window and sketches shapes for his next teapot on a napkin. The owner knows him well enough to ask after his latest firing. He tends to cradle his coffee the way he cradles a bowl, carefully and with both hands.

Pottery is slow, and he has come to love that about it. A single set of cups can take three weeks from wedging to glaze, with the kiln doing most of the waiting. He jots every firing temperature in a battered notebook that his late father once used for accounts.

The studio is rented by the hour, and the hours are getting harder to justify on his current wage. He sometimes wonders whether the money would be better spent elsewhere. Then he trims a foot ring on a bowl and the thought drifts off again.

A pot cracked in the kiln again this week, a clean split down the side that he will not get back. He stood over the shelves for a long while before sweeping up the pieces. His sister says he should give up, but he has started a new bowl anyway.

His grandmother kept a cupboard full of mismatched cups, each one a little lopsided. He inherited that cupboard and now adds his own wonky mugs to it. The cafe on the corner sells his cups with honey-coloured glaze, and people always ask where they came from.

He keeps a list taped to the studio door of the glazes he still wants to master. Crackle glaze is at the top, underlined twice. Rent is due on the first, so the list sometimes feels more like a hope than a plan.

Some mornings the pottery is the only thing that goes right. He centres the clay, opens it up, and pulls the walls up thin without collapsing them. The rest of the day can wait while he trims a cup and watches the curl of clay fall away.

Over the holidays he drove to his grandfather's village and found the old kick wheel in a barn. He spent an afternoon with dust in his hair, coaxing a small bowl from a lump of local clay. The bowl is now the centrepiece of his shelf at home.

The garden shed behind his house is half workshop and half sail loft. He stitches new batten pockets on a sewing machine older than he is. The sails hang from the rafters like pale flags waiting for spring.

A week-long cruise through the islands was his big holiday this year. Every morning the anchor came up with a clatter, and every evening he cooked a pasta dish on the gimbaled stove. He sleeps deeply in a bunk that rocks gently all night.

He reads the weather forecast the way other people read the sports pages. Pressure drops and wind shifts are things he talks about at dinner. Last week the news mentioned a storm front and he spent the whole evening on the radar app.

Sailing for him began as a cheap way to get out on the water without owning a motorboat. Now he owns three boats and an opinion about each of them. His cousin still thinks he is slightly mad for spending weekends in wet oilskins.

The sail repair kit lives under his kitchen sink, which annoys his partner no end. Sail tape, a palm, and a bag of heavy thread are his tools of choice. He patched a torn genoa on the dining table last winter.

His grandfather built a wooden dinghy in the backyard, and that boat still hangs in his own garage. He sands the old hull every spring and fits new oarlocks. Sailing it feels like a conversation with a man who has been gone for years.

Light winds frustrate him more than anything, and he will happily motor back to the mooring rather than drift. He admits this to nobody except his brother. Still, on a good day he sails in silence for hours and forgets to check his phone.

The yacht club bar is where he tells the same story about the capsize every season. Each retelling gets slightly more dramatic than the last. Someone always asks him to make the chowder, and he never refuses.

Winter is the hardest season for him, since the boat stays on its stands and the harbour turns grey. He spends the cold evenings rereading old sailing books by the fire. Occasionally he rigs a model yacht on the kitchen table just to keep his hands busy.

A friend asked him once why he needed so many ropes, and he spent twenty minutes explaining the difference between a halyard and a sheet. The friend nodded politely and changed the subject. He was secretly delighted to have an audience.

He keeps a logbook in the cabin, filled with pencilled notes about wind speed, tides, and the odd wildlife sighting. Seals appear most mornings near the point. He has never once remembered to write down the name of the bird that dived onto his hat.

Sailing taught him patience, which is more than his work ever managed. He spends hours watching the telltales flutter on the jib and adjusting the sheets by inches. Back on land he is much calmer about traffic jams and difficult customers.

A cheap old plastic dinghy sits in the corner of his garden shed, waiting for children who never visit. He polishes it every March anyway. Maybe next summer, he tells himself, the neighbours' kids will come down to the lake.

Most of his friends picture a yacht when they hear the word sailing, but he mostly skips about on a small catamaran. He finds it more fun than anything with a cabin and a fridge. The trapeze harness leaves bruises on his hips every single weekend.
